a: An LLM that runs in a loop: it reasons about the goal, chooses a tool or action, observes the result and repeats until done. The application executes the tools; the model only proposes calls.

q: How does function / tool calling work?
a: You pass tool definitions (name, description, JSON schema). The model returns a structured call with arguments instead of text; your code validates and executes it, returns the result as a message, and the model continues.

q: Why LangGraph over a simple LangChain chain?
a: LangGraph models the application as a state graph with typed state, nodes, conditional edges and cycles, so loops, retries, routing and multi-agent setups are explicit. It adds checkpointing (memory, resume, time travel) and human-in-the-loop interrupts, which production agents need.

q: Workflow or agent: how do you choose?
a: If the steps are known, use a workflow: predictable, cheaper, easier to test. Use an agent only where the sequence of actions genuinely depends on intermediate results. Many good systems are workflows with a router or a small agentic step.
Reason + Act: the model alternates a thought, an action (tool call) and an observation (tool result), building up information step by step before giving a final answer.

Model Context Protocol: an open standard for exposing tools, data resources and prompts to LLM applications through MCP servers. Any compatible client can use any server, replacing one-off integrations.

q: How do you make agents reliable in production?
a: Few well-described tools with strict schemas, argument validation, iteration/time/cost limits, loop detection, least-privilege credentials, human approval for risky actions, fallbacks on tool errors, full tracing, and evaluation of trajectories (right tool, right arguments) as well as final answers.

q: How do you add memory to an agent?
a: Short-term: keep the conversation in the graph state, trimming or summarising older turns. Long-term: write durable facts to a store (vector DB or key-value) and retrieve them when relevant. LangGraph checkpointers persist state per thread.

q: Does the LLM execute the tool?
a: No. The model only outputs a structured call (name + JSON arguments). Your application validates and executes it, which is where you enforce permissions, read-only access, timeouts and input checks.

q: How do you evaluate an agent?
a: Task success on a fixed set of realistic tasks, trajectory quality (right tools, valid arguments, no wasted steps), efficiency (steps, tokens, cost, latency) and safety (no forbidden actions, correct escalations).
Start single. Multi-agent (supervisor with specialists) helps when sub-tasks need clearly different tools or prompts, but adds cost, latency and hand-off failures.

q: How do you stop an agent from looping forever?
a: Max iterations / recursion limit, token and cost budgets, timeouts, detection of repeated identical tool calls, and clear tool error messages so the model can change course.
